newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO in crisis, Clinton meets Mubarak.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO in crisis, Clinton meets Mubarak.

text.p: Palestinians clashed with Israeli soldiers in the West Bank on Monday, deepening a crisis over an Israeli troop redeployment plan that Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat angrily rejected as a trick.

Near the West Bank town of Hebron, at least 10 Palestinians were injured by troops who used clubs and guns to beat back about 100 Arabs who tried to stop workers from opening a road for Jewish settlers, witnesses said.
The clash was the first serious outbreak of Israeli-Arab violence since Arafat spurned an Israeli decision to hand over another nine percent of the West Bank to PLO rule.
Hours after the violence erupted, Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai held talks with Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo in an apparent bid to ease tensions.
A spokesman for Mordechai declined to give details of the meeting, saying only "current events" were on the agenda.

Earlier Rabbo warned of a possible repetition of violence that erupted in September after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu opened a new entrance to an archaeology tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem.
"The policy of Mr Netanyahu and his government will lead us to the abyss, will lead us to very dangerous things which we are all trying to avoid," Abed Rabbo told Israel Radio.

In Washington, U.S. President Bill Clinton met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who has said he would ask Clinton to pressure Israel into reversing a recent decision to build 6,500 Jewish homes in East Jerusalem.
Palestinians want East Jerusalem -- captured by Israel in the 1967 war -- as the capital of a future state but Israel says the whole city will always be the Jewish state's capital.

The settlement plan, coupled with Israel's decision on Friday to turn over nine percent of the West Bank as the first part of a three-part withdrawal outlined in the 1995 peace deal, has infuriated Palestinians.

In a sign of growing Arab anger, the chief Palestinian peace negotiator handed Arafat his resignation on Monday, PLO officials said. Arafat has yet to accept the decision by Mahmoud Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen.

"There is a real crisis because there is a clear breaching to what had been agreed upon," Arafat told reporters in Gaza, referring to the redeployment. He called the Israeli move "a trick and a conspiracy against the peace process".
Palestinians wanted 30 percent and a say in determining the scope of this and two other pullbacks from mainly rural areas of the West Bank mandated by Israel-PLO peace deals.
Mubarak is the third Middle Eastern leader to meet Clinton at the White House in the past month, following Netanyahu's visit on February 13 and Arafat's on March 3.
Jordan's King Hussein is due in Washington for talks next Tuesday.
But Israel defended its right to set the terms of withdrawal.

"It is a matter of Israeli implementation, not for Palestinian-Israeli negotiation, and the Palestinians were the first to admit this in their discussions with us," said Dore Gold, a senior Netanyahu adviser.

Israeli security sources said the army has a plan to deploy tanks and snipers in the West Bank if clashes such as those that killed 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers six months ago when the tunnel in East Jerusalem was opened, break out again.
"I hope there will not be any riots or other violence but the defence authorities are prepared for all possibilities," Mordechai told reporters in Tel Aviv.
Netanyahu flew to Russia on Monday for an official visit and Israel Radio quoted a senior official on board his plane as saying Israel and the PLO "appeared to be headed towards a difficult crisis".
The nine-percent decision followed two other actions that irked Palestinians -- approval for the Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem and steps to shut down four PLO offices there.
Foreign Minister David Levy said he made clear to Abu Mazen in talks on Sunday that Israel would not reconsider building the settlement or negotiate the West Bank pullback.
But an Israeli official said Israel would not go ahead with the redeployment so long as the PLO, which currently has sole control of about three percent of the West Bank, rejected it.
